scenario_stem:
Kindred Vale Dairy Co is a private limited company in Country X founded 6 years ago by Renata Vidal. It bottles fresh milk and plain yoghurt for 25 local shops, employs 18 workers and produced 200,000 litres last year. Fixed costs were $120,000 and variable costs $0.40 per litre, giving an average cost of $1.00. It sells to local shops at $1.20 per litre.

A national supermarket chain has offered a three-year contract that would lift output to 320,000 litres a year. Fixed costs would rise only to $160,000, bulk buying of bottles and lids would cut variable costs by $0.05 per litre, and six extra staff would be needed. The supermarket would pay $1.05 per litre, and Renata must decide whether to sign the contract or keep supplying local shops.

The board is weighing two options. A new injection-moulding machine costing $600,000 would lift capacity to 60,000 helmets a year, cut variable cost to $7.50 and raise fixed costs to $330,000. A growers' co-operative has offered a two-year contract for 120 tonnes of tomatoes at $800 per tonne, compared with $1,000 per tonne bought weekly, a saving of $24,000 a year. scenario_stem:

Demand has grown by 15% a year for three years, and its two largest customers have asked about faster northern deliveries.

The board is considering a second northern factory, doubling capacity to 180,000 units a year. Fixed costs would rise to $3.24 million, while bulk buying of fabric would cut variable cost to $20 per unit. However, the order book is unconfirmed [k]: at today's 3.6 million tins, average cost would be about $0.38 and fixed costs of $660,000 would pressure cash flow until orders are signed [app], and demand below 3.6 million tins would push average cost back toward $0.43 [an]. Overall [eval], Eastport should install the line only once at least one supermarket chain commits in writing to extra volume — the potential $424,000 gain outweighs the loan risk if capacity is filled, but installing speculatively would risk debt service on underused machinery [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost and raise profit
Unfilled capacity and loan commitments create financial risk
application_max_2: At 3.6 million tins average cost is about $0.38; fixed costs $660,000; neither contract signed
analysis_max_2: $424,000 extra profit would recover the investment in about two years
Unconfirmed demand leaves fixed costs under-recovered and cash flow strained
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to securing a signed order first

scenario_stem:
Amberfield Packaging Ltd is a private limited company in Country X packing cardboard cartons for food producers. It has traded for 9 years, employs 46 workers and packed 1,000,000 cartons last year, earning revenue of $1.6 million. Fixed costs are $300,000, variable cost is $0.60 and average cost is $0.90.

A national grocery chain has shortlisted Amberfield to supply another 1,000,000 cartons a year, doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons. Serving it needs a second plant costing $500,000, which the bank would finance at 7.5% interest thanks to its track record; a start-up rival was quoted 11%. Fixed costs would rise to $520,000 and bulk buying would cut variable cost to $0.55. The chain would decide by next quarter, and Amberfield would need to begin building within six months to keep the contract.

questions.question_text: Define 'financial economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Financial economies of scale are the advantages larger or more established businesses gain when raising finance, such as lower interest rates and better access to loans and share issues. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Established/larger firms borrow more cheaply (lower interest rates)
Better access to finance: loans, debentures, share issues at lower cost

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the bank finance for the second plant.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cheaper borrowing than rivals [k]. At 7.5% interest the $500,000 loan costs $37,500 a year, while a start-up rival quoted 11% would pay $55,000 — saving $17,500 a year [app]. Reason 2: The finance unlocks rapid expansion [k]. A second plant doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons enables the grocery chain contract without waiting years to accumulate profit [app].

knowledge_max_2: Established firms get lower interest rates (financial economies of scale)
Access to finance enables investment that retained profit cannot fund quickly
application_max_2: 7.5% interest = $37,500 a year versus 11% = $55,000; saving $17,500 a year
Capacity doubles to 2,000,000 cartons; second plant costing $500,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the expansion could cause.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher fixed costs and debt [k]. Fixed costs rise to $520,000 and the $37,500 interest is an unavoidable yearly outflow [app], so profit could fall sharply if the grocery chain order is delayed or cut, even though average cost falls toward $0.81 [an]. Problem 2: Diseconomies of scale may appear [k]. Running two sites duplicates management and slows communication [app], which could cause packing errors or late deliveries to the national chain and risk the contract that justified the investment [an].

knowledge_max_2: Debt and higher fixed costs increase financial risk
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decisions in larger firms
application_max_2: Fixed costs rise to $520,000; $37,500 annual interest on the $500,000 loan
Two sites with duplicated management; national grocery chain contract
analysis_max_2: If the order slips, fixed costs and interest still fall due, cutting net profit below the $0.81 average-cost plan
Errors or late deliveries could lose the contract, leaving spare capacity and debt

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfield Packaging Ltd should borrow $500,000 and build the second plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Borrowing to expand brings financial economies of scale [k]: at 7.5%, interest is $37,500 a year — far cheaper than the 11% a start-up rival would pay — and doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons cuts average cost from $0.90 to $0.81 [app], lifting profit before interest from $700,000 to about $1.58 million [an]. However, the loan creates fixed commitments [k]: if the grocery chain order is smaller or later than expected, the $520,000 fixed costs and interest still fall due, and operating two sites could cause diseconomies of scale, such as slower communication and packing errors for the national chain [app], eroding the $0.09 saving per carton [an]. Overall [eval], Amberfield should proceed, because even after $37,500 interest, profit after interest of about $1.54 million comfortably exceeds $700,000 today — but it should secure the chain's order in writing before drawing the loan and phase the second plant's ramp-up to protect quality [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Financial economies: established firms borrow at lower interest rates
Debt and diseconomies of scale create expansion risk
application_max_2: 7.5% interest = $37,500 a year versus 11% ($55,000); average cost falls $0.90 to $0.81
Fixed costs rise to $520,000; profit before interest rises $700,000 to about $1.58 million; $500,000 loan
analysis_max_2: Doubling capacity spreads fixed costs and bulk buying cuts $0.05 per carton, lifting profit by about $880,000
Underfilled capacity or poor coordination raises average cost and threatens the national contract
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified position
Clear overall judgement with conditions (signed contract first, phased ramp-up)

scenario_stem:
Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd is a private limited company in Country X brewing elderflower and ginger cordials. It employs 28 staff, sells 750,000 bottles a year in 400 regional shops and earns revenue of $1.5 million. Fixed costs are $420,000, variable cost is $0.80 per bottle and marketing spending is $90,000 a year, reaching about 120,000 households. It is known locally for its distinctive glass swing-top bottles.

A media agency proposes a national television campaign costing $400,000 over 2 years, reaching an estimated 3 million households; sales could rise by 20%. Larkhill hopes a national supermarket listing would follow wider awareness. Alternatively, five separate regional television slots are priced at $120,000 each, and Larkhill could simply continue its local promotions.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Marketing economies of scale are the cost advantages gained when advertising and promotion costs are spread over a larger output, lowering the marketing cost per unit sold. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Cost of advertising/promotion spread over more units lowers marketing cost per unit
Example: one national campaign cheaper per customer than many regional campaigns

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the national television campaign.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A wider reach at lower cost per household [k]. The $400,000 campaign reaches an estimated 3 million households for about $0.13 each, versus $0.75 per household on the current local campaign [app]. Reason 2: Sales could rise nationally [k]. If sales grow by 20% to 900,000 bottles, revenue rises from $1.5 million to $1.8 million and the fixed campaign cost is spread over more bottles [app].

knowledge_max_2: One national campaign reaches more customers at lower marketing cost per customer
Higher sales volume spreads fixed marketing costs, lowering cost per unit
application_max_2: $0.13 per household ($400,000/3 million) versus $0.75 per household local spending
20% sales rise = 900,000 bottles; revenue $1.5 million to $1.8 million

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons Larkhill might keep its local promotions instead.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The campaign may not pay back [k]. At an extra $110,000 a year above current spending, Larkhill needs roughly 92,000 extra bottles a year just to break even [app] — about 12% growth — and if the forecast 20% fails, profit falls below today's $480,000 [an]. Reason 2: National reach may be wasted without distribution [k]. Advertising to 3 million households means little while bottles sell in only 400 regional shops [app], because unavailable stock turns awareness into lost sales rather than revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Marketing spend is a fixed cost; weak sales growth leaves it under-recovered
Advertising is ineffective without distribution to meet demand
application_max_2: Extra $110,000 a year required; break-even needs about 92,000 extra bottles (12%)
400 regional shops only; bottles/revenue at risk if national demand cannot be supplied
analysis_max_2: If growth is under 12%, the campaign adds cost without enough contribution to cover it
Awareness without stock loses sales and damages brand, wasting the $400,000

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd should spend $400,000 on the national campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The national campaign offers marketing economies of scale [k]: it reaches 3 million households at about $0.13 each — far cheaper than $0.75 per household locally — and saves $200,000 against five separate regional slots at $120,000 each [app], so if sales rise by 20% as forecast, the extra $1.20 contribution per bottle covers the extra spend within two years [an]. However, the risk of weak returns is real [k]: at only 10% sales growth, Larkhill gains just 75,000 bottles of contribution, about $90,000 a year, which fails to cover the extra $110,000 a year above current local spending [app], leaving Larkhill worse off than continuing its $90,000 local promotions [an]. Overall [eval], Larkhill should proceed only if national retailers sign listings and the agency stages payments — the reach and $200,000 saving versus regional slots justify the spend once distribution is secured; without it, local promotion remains safer [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Marketing economies of scale: wider reach at lower cost per customer
Marketing is a fixed cost; returns depend on distribution and sales growth
application_max_2: $0.13 per household nationally versus $0.75 locally; $200,000 cheaper than five regional slots at $120,000 each
At 10% growth contribution is about $90,000 a year, below the extra $110,000 a year cost
analysis_max_2: At 20% growth the extra contribution repays the additional spend within two years
Slow sales or poor distribution leaves the fixed campaign cost unrecovered
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to securing national distribution first

scenario_stem:
Kettle & Fern Tea Co is a private limited company in Country X grading and packing specialty teas. It employs 22 workers, blended 480 tonnes last year and is renowned for consistent quality, winning regular national awards for flavour and sourcing. Fixed costs are $1.44 million, variable cost is $5,000 per tonne and average cost is $8,000. Tea sells at $9,000 per tonne, giving revenue of $4.32 million.

The board wants a purpose-built plant costing $3 million, doubling capacity to 960 tonnes. Fixed costs would rise to $2.4 million, so average cost would fall to $7,500 per tonne. Confirmed orders total only 700 tonnes; the company's economist warns that beyond 1,200 tonnes, poor communication and low morale could push average cost back up.

questions.question_text: Define 'average fixed cost'.
questions.model_answer: Average fixed cost is the fixed cost of production divided by the number of units produced; it falls continuously as output rises because the same fixed costs are spread more thinly. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Average fixed cost = fixed costs / output
It falls as output increases because fixed costs are spread over more units

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the new plant would lower Kettle & Fern's average cost.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Fixed costs spread over more tonnes [k]. Average fixed cost falls from $3,000 per tonne at 480 tonnes to $2,500 per tonne at 960 tonnes [app]. Reason 2: Technical economies of scale from purpose-built machinery [k]. Doubling capacity to 960 tonnes cuts average cost from $8,000 to $7,500 per tonne [app].

knowledge_max_2: Spreading fixed costs over larger output lowers average fixed cost
Larger, modern machinery creates technical economies of scale
application_max_2: Average fixed cost falls $3,000 per tonne (480 tonnes) to $2,500 per tonne (960 tonnes)
Capacity doubles to 960 tonnes; average cost falls $8,000 to $7,500

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with building the new plant ahead of demand.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Confirmed demand is too low [k]. Orders total only 700 tonnes against capacity of 960 tonnes [app]; at 700 tonnes, average cost would be about $8,429 — higher than today's $8,000 — so the plant would lose money until sales grow [an]. Problem 2: Diseconomies of scale are threatened [k]. The economist warns that beyond 1,200 tonnes, poor communication and low morale push average cost back up [app], so costs could rise again just as the new plant reaches full capacity [an].

knowledge_max_2: Underused capacity raises average cost and erodes the benefit of expansion
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and low morale raise average cost at large scale
application_max_2: Confirmed orders of only 700 tonnes versus 960 tonnes capacity
Economist warns of diseconomies beyond 1,200 tonnes
analysis_max_2: At 700 tonnes average cost rises to about $8,429, making current volume better served by the old plant
Rising costs beyond 1,200 tonnes would reverse the falling average cost curve

questions.question_text: Do you think Kettle & Fern Tea Co should build the new plant now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building now captures technical economies of scale [k]: average cost falls from $8,000 to $7,500 per tonne at 960 tonnes, and profit could rise from $480,000 to about $1.44 million [app], making the $3 million investment recoverable within a few years [an]. However, confirmed orders are only 700 tonnes [k]: at that volume average cost would be about $8,429, worse than today, and output beyond 1,200 tonnes risks diseconomies of scale such as poor communication and low morale [app], so building ahead of demand gambles $3 million on unsigned sales [an]. Overall [eval], Kettle & Fern should delay construction until signed orders exceed roughly 800 tonnes — the point where average cost matches today's $8,000 — and meanwhile secure national distribution agreements, because proceeding at 700 tonnes would destroy the expected saving [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost and raise profit
Diseconomies of scale and underused capacity threaten large investments
application_max_2: Average cost falls $8,000 to $7,500; profit could rise $480,000 to $1.44 million; $3 million cost
Only 700 tonnes confirmed; at 700 tonnes average cost is about $8,429; diseconomies beyond 1,200 tonnes
analysis_max_2: At full capacity the $500 per tonne saving adds about $480,000 of annual profit
At 700 tonnes the higher average cost erases the gain and strains cash for loan repayments
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to achieving at least 800 tonnes of signed orders
